title: He emptied himself (Philippians 2:5–11)
hookLine: an early hymn: he took the form of a servant, humbled himself to death
carry: all the way down, for others

lines: ALL THE WAY DOWN, ALL THE WAY UP.
cards: In the middle of a letter from prison, Paul's writing suddenly changes rhythm. The sentences start to balance, line against line, like poetry.

Many scholars think Paul is quoting a hymn here, something the earliest Christians already sang, within a few decades of the crucifixion. If they're right, these six verses are among the oldest words about Jesus we have.
Some think Paul wrote them himself. Either way, the shape is unmistakable: a song that goes all the way down, and then all the way up.

teach.h: LET THIS MIND BE IN YOU.
teach.b: It begins: "Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus." Then the descent.

In the King James Bible: "Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men."
The Greek is shorter and sharper: ekenosen, he emptied himself. From that verb comes today's word, kenosis, self-emptying. He didn't treat equality with God as something to grab or cling to.

teach.h: DOWN TO THE DEATH OF THE CROSS.
teach.b: Then the steps keep going down: a servant, a human being. "he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross." The cross was the death Rome used for slaves and rebels. Then the turn.
"Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him."

teach.h: THEN UP: EVERY KNEE SHOULD BOW.
teach.b: All the way up: "That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow," in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord.
Those lines echo the prophet Isaiah, where God says every knee will bow to him; the hymn hears that promise fulfilled in Jesus.

What exactly did he empty himself of? Christians have asked that for centuries. Most churches teach that he didn't stop being God, but set aside the privileges, taking on our limits, our hunger, our death.
Some modern theologians have pushed the idea further. All agree on the direction: down, for others. And that's Paul's point for the Philippians.
Look to others, because this is the mind of Christ.

how: Many churches read Philippians 2:5–11 on Palm Sunday, and in some traditions people bow their heads at the name of Jesus, a custom drawn from this hymn.

games.q: you're telling the Philippians to stop chasing glory. what do you point to?
o: a hymn about Christ emptying himself.
games.why: "Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus", and then the hymn: all the way down, then all the way up.

practice: Think of something that needs doing that nobody wants to do and nobody will thank you for: a neighbor's trash cans, listening to someone everyone else avoids.
Notice the small voice that says that's not my job, and picture yourself doing it anyway, quietly, the way a servant would. If you pray, you can pray the hymn's first line: let this mind be in me.

wordCard.voice: Kenosis. Greek for self-emptying: the hymn's picture of Christ letting go of his rights and going all the way down, for others.

orig.note: Greek: he emptied. from kenos, empty. the noun kenosis, self-emptying, comes from this verb.

carryVoice: Your line: all the way down, for others. That's the shape of the song. Day six hundred sixty, done.
